chapter_theme: Joining good company: it washes out the faults of youth, raises the lowly as river water sanctifies sewage, protects the weak and hides meanness. Life's pain makes the company of the wise the thing to seek, and bad company ruins even the pure.
structure_note: 173 and 174 frame good company against the pain of birth; 175 to 178 give four images of the low raised by the high; 179 and 180 turn to the damage done by evil company.

171.reading: Faults committed in thoughtless youth, keeping company with the unruly and going astray, vanish once one joins good people who know the right way, as dew lets go of the grass when the sun grows hot.
171.nuance: Mudaliar names these faults the faults of association (சகவாச தோஷங்கள்). Company is both the cause of the wrong and its cure.

172.reading: Know the path of virtue; dread Death; bear the harsh words of others; guard against deceit; shun friendship with evildoers; and always take in the words of the great.
172.nuance: Mudaliar reads போற்றுமின் வஞ்சம் as preventing deceit from arising in oneself, and allows வாய்ச்சொல் to mean the blessing of the great.

173.reading: Since parting from those one is close to, grievous illness and ruin come together to all who take a body, O my heart, cling to those of great understanding who see that birth is bitter from its start.

positions.position: கேடு is harm or misfortune in general.
கேடு is death, completing the list of separation, illness and death.

173.nuance: The speaker addresses his own heart. The reason for seeking the wise is not their virtue but their insight into birth as suffering.

174.reading: Though birth, when thought through, is extremely bitter, no one would resent it if within it they could keep lasting friendship with people whose hearts practise goodness.
174.nuance: Mudaliar notes that 'if they can get it' (பெறின்) marks how rare such friendship is. The verse redeems birth without denying its pain.

175.reading: Town drain water that joins a great river loses its name and becomes holy water; consider: even those without lineage stand like a hill by joining the good.

176.reading: The hare in the bright moon is worshipped along with it in the sky; so those of slight worth gain worth by friendship with men as steady as a hill.
176.nuance: Mudaliar explains the hare as the moon's dark mark: no one removes the spot before worshipping the moon, so the flaw shares the honour.

177.reading: Water mixed with milk becomes milk and no longer shows its own colour; so, on inspection, the smallness of small people does not show when they join the greatness of the good.
177.nuance: The verse says the meanness is hidden, not removed. That is a weaker claim than 171, where faults vanish.

178.reading: Grass growing against a stump in a large field is not moved by the farmer's plough; so the anger of enemies cannot reach the weak who have joined good company.

179.reading: As paddy thrives by the goodness of its soil, the worthy flourish by the goodness of their own group; and worth is ruined by joining evil company, as a gale wrecks a sound ship.

positions.position: குலம் is the company one joins, keeping the verse within the chapter's theme.
positions.quote: த‌ம்த‌ம் குல‌ம் ந‌ல‌த்தால் - தாந்தாஞ் சேர்கிற‌ கூட்ட‌த்தின் நன்மையான்

positions.position: குலம் is the family one is born into; the worthy are formed by their birth.
positions.quote: தாம் பிறந்த குடியின் பெருமையால் உயர்ந்தோர் உருவாகின்றனர்

179.nuance: Pope's 'clanships' leans toward birth. Which reading one takes decides whether this verse agrees or collides with 195.

180.reading: Though spotless in mind, people are scorned for the company they keep: when a cleared field is set on fire, the fragrant sandal and the vengai burn with the rest.
180.nuance: The verse concerns reputation and fate together: the pure are blamed, and the fire also destroys them.

links.note: 455 says purity of mind and deed both lean on purity of company; 171 shows company acting on past deeds as well, clearing the faults of youth.
415 calls the words of the good a staff on slippery ground; 172 closes its six precepts with taking in the words of the great every day.
Both commend bearing others' harsh words; 159 ranks those who do it with renunciants, 172 lists it among the basic precepts.
Both treat birth as the thing to escape: 362 says if one must want, want not to be born, and 173 seeks out those who know birth is bitter.
173 declares birth bitter from the start. 174, placed next to it, grants that and adds that friendship with the good makes birth something no one would resent.
460 says there is no greater support than good company. 174 raises the stakes: good company is what reconciles a person to being born at all.

Both use water changed by what it joins. In 452 water takes on the nature of its soil, as a mind takes on its company; in 175 sewage takes the name of the sacred river, as the lowly take the standing of the good.
Both use the moon's dark spot. In 151 the moon tolerates its flaw and the noble cannot; in 176 the flaw is worshipped because it sits in the moon.
Milk and its mixture, in opposite directions: in 1000 good milk is spoiled by a bad vessel, as wealth by a graceless owner; in 177 water is absorbed into milk, as the small into the great.
446: enemies can do nothing to one who walks with the worthy. 178 gives the image of grass the plough cannot uproot because it grows against a stump.
458 says that even the worthy, whose minds are good, are protected by good company. 179 gives the converse: their worth is wrecked by bad company.
453 says what a person is called comes from their company; 180 says the pure in mind are scorned because of theirs.
The same mechanism run both ways: in 177 the mean are hidden by the great, in 180 the pure are blackened by the bad.

source_issues: 171: the Shanmuganar field also contains the text of 172 and Shanmuganar's commentary on it; 172 is marked not aligned for Shanmuganar, so that commentary was not used.
